whyScene: The objective is a traversal order and a stack that grows then shrinks. The order and the LIFO discipline exist only over time, and the misconception that backtracking is a fresh search is refuted by showing the same stack popping while the visited marks stay put.
layout: Graph on the left two thirds: A(480,112), B(300,244), C(700,252), D(480,400), edges A-B, A-C, B-D, D-C drawn behind white node discs so labels stay legible. Stack box at x=800..920, four slots, bottom slot A, top slot C.

beats.beat: Move to C, push C: depth four.
C pops: both its neighbours are already on the path.
B pops after D; the visited marks stay.
A pops: its remaining neighbour C is already visited.
Visit-order replay A, B, D, C.

interaction.prompt: A is on the stack. Continue to follow one branch.
Depth three: A, B, D. Will DFS open C next, or backtrack to A first?
At C, both neighbours are already on the path. What should DFS do instead of pushing a node twice?
The stack has shrunk back to A. Does that undo the visits to B and D?
Continue to replay the visit order.

misconceptionMoves.move: The stack reaches depth four (A, B, D, C) while C, a neighbour of the start, is only reached at the end; the visit order is A, B, D, C, not A, B, C, D.
Pops 11.2 to 15.6 shrink the same stack and leave every visited mark in place; no node is re-explored.

correctnessChecks: Frontier is LIFO: the most recently pushed node is the one expanded next (B before C at A; D before C at B).
The visited/path test blocks a repeat at C, whose neighbours A and D are both already visited.
No shortest-path claim: the closing line says DFS is not a shortest-path search, and C is reached at depth four though adjacent to A.
